title: Health-care cash has to be better spent
article: A big infusion of cash into the health-care system may be just what Doc Romanow ordered, but whether that will be the long-term cure for an ailing -- if not critical -- patient will be determined over the next few years.

Roy Romanow, at least, has an easy out. If the feds don't come up with the millions more in funding he calls for, he can't be blamed. What the former Saskatchewan premier has done is put the onus for improving the system -- reduced waiting list, better access to diagnostic services, etc. -- on the federal government.

It's unfortunate that his cure is all about increasing the amount of money in the system. There were many other good recommendations, but they will get lost in the dollar figures -- $15 billion here, another billion there. One of the key points will be ensuring the public that their tax dollars are being spent as wisely as possible, and to be benefit of as many Canadians as possible.

Of course, this is coming from a premier who didn't want the provincial auditor examining all of the province's finances, only those he wanted the public to know about -- and never anything to do with the Crown corporations.
How much do you expect the federal and provincial governments to show when it comes to health-care spending? They will do everything in their power to ensure the best possible spin.

In Prince Albert, the health authority is looking at reducing beds in the mental health ward while spending dollars on parking lots. The questions about the accountability are justified when funds are being spent on improving parking lots instead of improving real health services.
A coroner's jury made a few recommendations after hearing evidence about an incident in which Keldon McMillan was shot to death by police south of Wakaw in May 2001.

While there were some valid issues raised about how better communications between Saskatoon city police and the RCMP might have helped, in the end is was very apparent that McMillan's actions are the reason he is dead.

McMillan had been drinking and there was evidence that he may have taken cocaine. He had a history of violence and had shot a police dog. He was shot after aiming at police. They feared for their own lives and fired at him.
The jury recommended the use of tasers, a type of stun-gun that uses electric shock. But McMillan was too far away, and what happens if the shock doesn't work? We have a dead police officer.

Inquiries are necessary whenever police or corrections are involved in a fatality. It helps keep the system transparent. But what no jury can ever recommend is better judgment by the individual in trouble with the law. Ultimately, an individual has to be responsible for their own actions and the consequences of those actions.
